name: Melanotan tanning protocol

card.summary: A forum-described routine for using melanotan peptides to darken skin, in which users build up a tan during an initial 'loading' period and then keep it with a lower-frequency maintenance period, for a sunless tanned look.
card.note: Melanotan products are unapproved and unregulated; health agencies have issued warnings.

quick.overview:
The Melanotan tanning protocol is the community name for how people structure melanotan II (MT2) use: a loading phase to build pigmentation, followed by a maintenance phase to hold it. The goal is a darker, more even tan without prolonged sun exposure.

Melanotan II is a synthetic analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone that stimulates melanin production through melanocortin receptors. It was developed at the University of Arizona in the 1980s but was never marketed as a drug, and no trial-validated tanning schedule exists.
quick.how: Users in forums describe the general pattern of an initial period of repeated administration while pigmentation builds, often alongside some UV exposure, then spacing the use out to maintain colour. Specific amounts and injection details are deliberately not covered here.
quick.risks: Health agencies including the UK MHRA (2008), the Danish and Irish medicines regulators and the US FDA have warned against unregulated melanotan products. Reported effects include flushing, nausea, appetite loss and spontaneous erections, and darkening of moles and freckles. Evidence on melanoma risk is unsettled, and some case reports coincided with heavy sun or sunbed use.

lead: The Melanotan tanning protocol, sometimes called MT2 loading, is a pattern of use discussed in online tanning and looksmaxxing communities: a loading phase in which users build up skin pigmentation, followed by a maintenance phase that holds it. People follow it to get a sunless tan that improves skin tone and complexion in the way a natural tan does.

Melanotan II is a synthetic analogue of the hormone alpha-MSH. It acts as a non-selective agonist at melanocortin receptors MC1, MC3, MC4 and MC5, and stimulates melanin production via MC1 [1]. It was developed in the 1980s by University of Arizona scientists and never marketed as a drug; its sister compound melanotan I (afamelanotide) is FDA-approved for a rare light-sensitivity disorder [1]. The loading and maintenance structure comes from community practice rather than a clinical trial schedule.

angle.text: Users aim for a deeper, more even tan without relying on sun or sunbeds alone. The two-phase approach is a community convention for reaching and holding the colour.

paras: The protocol describes timing rather than a product: an initial intensive period, then a reduced-frequency period. It is a user convention, and published trials have not tested it [1].

Melanotan II activates melanocortin receptors. Its tanning effect comes through MC1 and melanogenesis, while effects on appetite and sexual arousal are linked to other receptors such as MC4 [1]. Development of the compound as a sexual-dysfunction drug ended in 2000 when its developer pursued bremelanotide, a related drug later approved as Vyleesi for low sexual desire in premenopausal women [1][2].

Common effects include facial flushing, nausea, vomiting, yawning, stretching, reduced appetite and erections in men; moles and freckles may darken reversibly [1]. A 2013 review found no conclusive evidence that it causes melanoma, and a 2021 review attributed higher melanoma risk among users to added UV exposure from tanning, though some reported melanomas coincided with heavy sunbathing or sunbed use [1].
Agencies in Denmark, the UK (MHRA, 2008), Ireland (2009) and Norway have warned about the products, and the FDA sent a warning letter to a laboratory in 2009 [1].
Melanotan I (afamelanotide) and the related bremelanotide have been studied in clinical programmes, but not the loading and maintenance routine described here [1].

timeline.event: Melanotan I and II developed at the University of Arizona [1]
Development of melanotan II as a drug stops as bremelanotide is pursued [1]
Health agencies begin warning against melanotan products [1]
